newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian rebels seize initiative in long war.
newsitem.headline: Colombian rebels seize initiative in long war.

text.p: A recent wave of leftist guerrilla violence has left Colombians reeling as the scales appear to tip in favour of Latin America's largest and oldest insurgency after more than three decades of war.

"Is the War Being Lost?" That question, posed in a headline splashed Sunday across the frontpage of El Tiempo -- Colombia's leading newspaper -- has no simple answer in a country where guerrillas and the army have been locked in a stalemate for most of the past 30 years.
Diplomats say the military has definitely lost the momentum, however, as guerrillas flex their muscles like never before.

Nearly 100 soldiers and police have been killed in about a fortnight in one of the bloodiest rebel offensives since the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) and National Liberation Army (ELN) -- Colombia's two leading rebel groups -- were founded in the mid-1960s.

Adding insult to injury, the FARC seized more than 60 soldiers as "prisoners of war" after overrunning a military base in the country's southwest jungle on August 30 and killing 27 troops. It announced in a communique on Saturday that it would be willing to begin negotiations toward the prisoners release in about 10 days, but the government, clearly humiliated by the hostage situation, said there was nothing to discuss.

"They (rebels) have shown a capacity for destruction that's unprecedented in the life of our nation," Prosecutor-General Alfonso Valdivieso said on Saturday, referring not just to the mounting government death toll but to a recent wave of rebel sabotage attacks and guerrilla blockades halting transportation in 15 of Colombia's 32 provinces.

Rebels have also been blamed by Valdivieso, Colombia's most respected public figure and the sort of strong-arm man many would like as president, for orchestrating a peasant revolt that spread this week from three southern provinces to Norte de Santander in the north, against the government's U.S.-backed drug crop eradication programme.

Vice President Humberto de la Calle said, in an open letter to President Ernesto Samper urging him to resign last Thursday, that the central government appeared completely unable to halt an unprecedented rebel threat to "democratic stability." Samper's government has been weakened by the scandal stemming from his alleged ties to drug lords.
"The security forces not only seem incapable of guaranteeing people's safety but must now watch as their own men are submitted to humiliating kidnappings," De la Calle said.

De la Calle is expected to resign from the vice presidency this week, so his criticism of the country's deteriorating security situation and what he describes as the virtual power vacuum might be dismissed as politically motivated by some. His concerns have been echoed by many political analysts, however.

A Western diplomat, citing military intelligence reports, said recently that Colombia's rebels -- who were about 10,000-strong in 1994 -- were expected to double their armies by mid-1998. The Colombian army, meanwhile, is about 120,000-strong and its commander, Gen. Harold Bedoya, said in a recent interview that he needed three times as many men to counter the growing threat posed by rebels.

The army, likened by one Western military expert to the rag-tag U.S. force that pursued Pancho Villa across the Rio Grande in 1916, also has just 35 helicopters for moving troops across Colombia's rugged mountainous terrain and jungles.
"One of the few things certain in Colombia is that the security situation is going from bad to worse," the diplomat said. "The military is strictly reactive."

De la Calle and others argue that Samper, who has endured repeated calls for his resignation, lacks the credibility and moral authority to be effective as commander-in-chief, especially since his alleged ties to drug lords have given guerrillas a new banner to carry in their war against the state.

Underscoring that view, the El Espectador newspaper said in its lead editorial on Sunday that Samper has essentially done nothing while Colombia burned around him. "The country is disintegrating in the shaky and inept hands of our leaders," it said.
